newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai raids on brokerages trigger criticisms.
newsitem.headline: Thai raids on brokerages trigger criticisms.

text.p: Police raids on two foreign brokerage houses suspected of possible involvement in rumours about Thai banks have left an unpleasant atmosphere in the equities industry.

Some analysts joined the local press and opposition politicians in criticising the raids on Bangkok offices of ABN-AMRO Hoare Govett Asia and Capital Nomura Securities Plc on Friday, saying they could further dampen bearish sentiment in the battered Thai economy.

"They were too heavy handed in conducting the raids. I am sure the two companies would have cooperated on requests in providing copies of what police were looking for, if they had them," a senior analyst at a Thai securities firm said.

Deputy Interior Minister Chalerm Yubamrung said in parliament on Thursday he ordered the raids after obtaining information that fax messages stating that the central bank planned to suspend medium and small Thai banks might have originated from the two companies.
The central bank denied the bank suspension rumours late last week.

Bangkok Metropolitan Bank Plc, Siam City Bank Plc, First Bangkok City Bank Plc, Laem Thong Bank Plc, and Union Bank of Bangkok Plc, have all denied they were potential targets of suspension by the government.

Both ABN-AMRO and Capital Nomura denied that they had been responsible for the rumours against Thai banks. Capital Nomura said on Friday that police searching its office did not find evidence of its involvement in the rumours.
A senior police officer said on Thursday executives of the two firms could face a maximum seven-year jail term if their firms were found to have spread rumours damaging the Thai economy.
"The raids would make us more sensitive to how the authorities feel but they would not stop us from saying what we want to say. There are alternative ways of saying things," a foreign analyst said.

Asked if the raids would have negative implication on future foreign investment in the Thai stock market, he said: "They were disappointing but I do not think they would lead to any boycott. People still have to do business."
Opposition member of parliament Sukhumphan Bharipat said the raids would destroy Thailand's long standing image of allowing a free flow of information.

"They just wanted to find scapegoats for problems facing the economy. The raids, especially at Capital Nomura, embarrassed Finance Minister Thanong (Bidaya) while he was in Japan," another Thai analyst said.
Thanong and central bank governor Rerngchai Marakanond are in Tokyo to brief Japanese government officials and bankers on problems faced by the Thai economy and its financial sector.

Thailand is going through its worst economic slump in more than a decade with severe problems in its financial and property sectors. On July 2, the authorities floated the baht, which led to a de facto devaluation of between 15 and 20 percent.

Thai business newspaper Krungthep Thurakij said in a front-page editorial: "Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh must be held responsible (for the raids which)...should be regarded as an act detrimental to the economy, a decision that will strongly erode foreign confidence and aggravate an economic situation already on the edge of an abyss."
Local journalists also said that getting industry analysts to go on the record with comments critical of the Thai authorities was becoming harder because some of them feared repercussions.
